content:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen, a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a cubic-kilometer detector composed of thousands of optical sensors buried in Antarctic ice. But why is the IceCube group going through all the trouble to build a massive array of subterranean detectors in Antarctica?

The primary goal of IceCube is to detect neutrinos — particles named by Italian physicist Enrico Fermi, meaning “little neutral one.” As the name suggests, neutrinos are small — current research caps the neutrino mass at roughly a millionth the mass of an electron; neutrinos also carry no charge, thus they are electrically “neutral.”

The existence of the neutrino was first hypothesized in 1930 by Wolfgang Pauli, one of the architects of quantum theory, in an effort to resolve a standing paradox in physics: beta decay. Beta decay is one type of radioactive decay — the same mechanism that drives carbon dating and positron emission tomography (P.E.T) scans. Prior to Pauli’s proposition of the neutrino, beta decay confused and unsettled physicists because, unlike the two other forms of radioactive decay, the particle emitted in beta decay — an electron — was found experimentally to have a continuous spectrum of possible energies.

This finding was alarming because the decay itself was supposed to have a fixed total energy, and accounting only for the nucleus of the atom and this variable energy of the emitted electron seemed to imply energy was disappearing. Pauli remedied this by proposing the neutrino, which he accounted for having gone undetected by attributing it to electric neutrality, small mass and extraordinarily weak interaction with other matter. Considering the neutrino as a second byproduct of beta decay allows the total energy to be shared by the electron and the neutrino, making the continuous range of energies for the electron valid.

Pauli was later proven experimentally to be right, but in a strange contention with his own initial beliefs about the detectability of the neutrino, Pauli famously said, “I have done a terrible thing. I have postulated a particle that cannot be detected.” 

Today, cutting-edge neutrino detectors like IceCube aim to consistently accomplish what Pauli bet was impossible. Neutrino detection still poses significant challenges, though, because neutrinos interact so weakly with all other matter; a neutrino can travel through a lightyear, or roughly six trillion miles, of solid lead without disturbing a single atom. 

Even crazier, neutrinos are the most abundant particle in the universe — about 100 trillion neutrinos are passing through your body this very second. This elusiveness of the neutrino is where IceCube and other neutrino detectors need to get creative.

Having the detector in the ice has two main advantages for the IceCube observatory. One is that the ice helps to reduce the number of background particles, particularly atmospheric muons produced by cosmic rays. Even with this background suppression, IceCube requires an enormous number of individual detectors in order to monitor the entire cubic kilometer of ice — 5160 optical sensors, to be exact. 

The second advantage of the ice is directly related to IceCube’s method of neutrino detection: The transparent glacial ice provides a massive, clear volume for neutrinos to interact and enables the optical detector modules to detect the light emitted. These detectors are sensitive to flashes of blue light produced when neutrinos interact with atomic nuclei in the ice, creating secondary charged particles that travel faster than light can travel through the ice. This phenomenon, known as Cherenkov radiation, allows IceCube to detect neutrinos indirectly.

Halzen is the principal investigator for this international collaboration, and the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences emphasized his proposal of this one-of-a-kind detector in 1988. One particularly astonishing thing about the neutrinos IceCube detects is that the detector can use the spatial and temporal distribution of light emitted to inform researchers about the energy of the neutrino that produced the charged particle and approximately where it came from.

Neutrinos are also unique sources of astrophysical data. Since neutrinos interact so weakly with other matter and carry no charge, they can travel from distant cosmic sources with little absorption or magnetic deflection. This “resiliency” of the neutrino makes it a remarkably good carrier of information, and therefore neutrinos can be used to indirectly learn about the environments in which they were produced.

A notable discovery made by the IceCube Collaboration was the detection of a neutrino that seemed to originate from a blazar, which is a type of active galactic nucleus — the extremely energetic central regions of galaxies — that have relativistic jet streams oriented toward the Earth that emit a vast number of particles with high energies. The detected astrophysical neutrinos themselves have immense energies — some are many times that of what is produced in CERN’s Large Hadron Collider, the world’s highest-energy particle collider.

Professor Halzen reflected on the long journey of bringing the IceCube detector to fruition in an interview with a member of the Nobel Prize outreach team. He underlined the improbability of the detector coming together and how much he appreciates his collaborators and UW-Madison for taking a chance on the idea, given that there weren’t any guarantees that it would work. Halzen remarked, “In fact, my main reaction to this project over time was not proud but was surprised. You know, I gave a talk very early in the project at a conference in Venice where I said, ‘This is a detector, Deo volente,’ which means ‘God willing.’” He explained that the project faced many obstacles and uncertainties, such as not knowing in advance if their method of drilling into the ice would be successful and if the ice would be transparent enough to detect the light at all. Halzen and the IceCube Collaboration ultimately prevailed over these many challenges, representing a monumental triumph in neutrino detection and astronomy, with Halzen’s contributions earning him the Nobel Prize.
